Gold isn't breaking out. It's waiting.

Bullion closed the week near $4,061 an ounce — up about 2% across five sessions, but still on the wrong side of the $4,100 line it has been probing for two weeks. That's not a breakout; it's a high plateau. The posture of a market waiting for someone else to move first.

This week, that someone is the Federal Reserve. The policy committee meets July 28–29, and the consensus expects it to hold rates steady. A hold keeps real yields roughly where they are — neither the tailwind nor the brake that would settle gold's direction. So the metal sits on its plateau, coiled, waiting for the signal.

A 10% tariff sounds small — until you see which lane it lands on.

India cuts and polishes somewhere around ninety percent of the world's diamonds by piece count, and it sends a huge slice of that output to American buyers. So when a 10% duty on Indian polished took effect on July 24, it didn't hit the highest rate on the board — it hit the single busiest lane in the entire polished trade.

And it landed at the worst possible moment. The men who own the wheels in Surat already had the least room to give: rough has been cheap, polished prices soft, and midstream margins thin for two years. A duty on top compresses the exact margin that was already the problem. Surat absorbs it, passes it on, or slows down — and none of those are painless.

Two numbers that used to move together are now moving apart — and the space between them was the whole watch trade.

Swiss brands opened 2026 with US retail increases of about 7%, led by Rolex, Tudor and Audemars Piguet. Meanwhile the secondary market spent the year sliding, with index trackers putting the broad decline near 8% and both Rolex and Patek Philippe touching two-year lows.

The list price went up. The street price went down. The gap between them is the subject — because that gap is where the last cycle's speculation lived. At the 2022 peak, a steel sports Rolex behaved like an asset, trading far above list. As the premium compresses, it stops behaving like one and starts behaving like a watch.
